summary: A 1974 survey of how far different sites had gotten in implementing the new Telnet protocol on their servers. It is a status snapshot, not a specification. It updates RFC 702 and is itself updated by RFC 679.

plainLanguage.summary: This report checks which ARPANET server hosts had implemented the new Telnet protocol. It records the survey results and the options each server supported.

questions: how many hosts had new telnet in 1974
subtitle: A December 1974 survey of new-protocol Telnet server support across ARPANET hosts.

tldr.problem: The report tracks how many listed server hosts could use the new Telnet protocol and how they configured it.
tldr.mechanism: A survey program and manual checks gathered results as seen from the new-protocol user Telnet at BBNA on December 4, 1974.
tldr.outcome: 16 of 37 server hosts had an implementation. The unit metadata says this RFC updates RFC 702 and was updated by RFC 679.

today: RFC 669 is a dated snapshot with status listed as Unknown. The unit metadata says it updates RFC 702 and was updated by RFC 679.

sections.title: Changes Since the Earlier Survey
sections.content:
The author says the appearance of new-protocol servers has progressed slowly. The listed changes include new servers at SRI-AI, USC-ISI and USC-ISIB; SDC-LAB returning to the network; and additions or changes to the host list.

SDC-CC and HAWAII-500 were listed as coming onto the network with unknown status. SDAC-44 was removed from the server-host list, LONDON was added, and BBN-TENEXD became host 162 instead of 205.
sections.plainLanguage: The report first lists hosts that joined, returned, changed number or left the server list. Some new hosts could not yet be checked.

sections.title: Survey Results
sections.content:
The summary counts 37 server hosts. Of these, 16 had a new-protocol implementation, 19 had none and two had unknown status. Among the 16 implementations, nine used the new protocol on socket 27 and the old one on socket 1; six used the new protocol on both sockets; and one used it only on socket 1.

The results came from a survey program run at various times and a few manual checks. They show how the servers appeared to the survey program at BBNA on December 4, 1974.
sections.plainLanguage: 16 of the 37 listed servers had the new protocol. 19 did not, and the survey could not determine the status of two.

sections.title: Sockets and Telnet Options
sections.content:
The table shows each server's host number and name, its protocol on socket 1 and socket 27, and any new-protocol options. X means there is no server at that socket, and a question mark means the status was not ascertained.

I followed by a number marks an option the server implements incoming to the user; O marks an option outgoing from the user. The report lists options 0 Transmit-Binary, 1 Echo, 3 Suppress-Go-Ahead and 6 Timing-Mark. An asterisk notes a server that gives improper responses to some option requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is a checklist for each host. It shows which Telnet version and options the survey found on each socket.

references.text: RFC 702, the earlier Telnet server survey whose summary this report updates.
